title: ScaleEnv: Scaling Environment Synthesis from Scratch for Generalist Interactive Tool-Use Agent Training
one_liner: Create many interactive training environments from scratch, test them automatically, and expand tool dependencies until each task is complete and solvable.
lead: A tool-using agent improves when it can practice inside many interactive environments because each action changes the world and reveals what the next step should be. Building those environments by hand is slow, and many generated environments break in small but fatal ways. This paper presents ScaleEnv, a system that builds environments from scratch, tests them procedurally, and verifies that each task can really be solved with the available tools.

problem.h2: Generalist agents need many places to practice, but interactive environments are scarce
paras: A generalist tool-use agent must adapt to many domains, many tool sets, and many multi-step tasks. Static instruction-answer pairs do not teach this well because the agent needs to act, observe the new state, and plan the next action. That requires interactive environments where actions have real consequences.

Existing environment synthesis methods usually fail in one of two ways. They either produce a small set of polished domains that do not cover enough variety, or they generate many domains that quietly break because tools are missing, states are inconsistent, or tasks ask for outcomes that cannot be achieved. Training on broken environments teaches the wrong lessons because the agent cannot tell whether failure came from its own policy or from a faulty world.

callout.html: Scale environment diversity without losing reliability, because agents need both breadth of practice and tasks that are actually executable.

steps.text: Create a new environment with objects, states, tools, and transition rules.
Propose goals the agent should accomplish inside that environment.
Check whether state updates, tool outputs, and observations remain internally consistent after actions.
If a goal requires tools or prerequisites that are missing, add them until the action chain can be completed.
Use executable action verification to retain tasks that can actually be solved with the environment's tool set.

paras: The paper changes how training environments are produced. Instead of relying on a small library of manually authored worlds, it builds worlds from scratch and treats verification as part of generation, not as a separate cleanup stage.
object.object: how environments are synthesized and verified

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: environment validity under action sequences
hidden.name: Executable completeness
paras: Executable completeness means that a task is not only stated but also reachable through a valid chain of actions in the environment. A domain can look detailed on paper while still failing this test if one required tool is absent, one state transition is broken, or one observation rule hides information the agent must know.

ScaleEnv estimates executable completeness by testing the environment with procedural checks and by expanding the dependency graph of required tools. If a goal says 'send the report', the system verifies that earlier actions such as opening the workspace, editing the file, and accessing the send tool are all possible in sequence. A task is kept only when that full chain can execute.

heat.caption: Darker cells show the parts that determine whether a task can really be executed from start to finish.

reads.html: A task counts only if an agent could actually finish it by pressing the available buttons in the right order.

The framework validates solvability through dependency expansion and executable rollouts, because realistic tool-use training requires action traces that can be completed inside the synthesized world.

mechanism.h2: Why verified synthesis scales better than hand-building
paras: Environment diversity matters because a generalist agent learns broader habits only when it sees many different task structures, tool interfaces, and failure modes. A small fixed set of environments can teach narrow routines, but it leaves the agent brittle when the benchmark changes domain or tool layout.

Naive large-scale generation fails because interactive worlds have hidden constraints. One missing prerequisite can make a task unsolvable, and one incorrect transition can make the state drift away from reality after several steps. ScaleEnv handles this by turning verification into part of the generator itself: each draft world is stress-tested, and missing dependencies are added before the task is accepted.

This improves training because the agent's experience becomes trustworthy. When the agent fails, the failure is more likely to come from its own planning rather than from a broken environment. That matters for generalization because consistent feedback lets the agent learn reusable action patterns across many domains instead of memorizing accidental quirks of faulty worlds.

math.words: A synthesized task is accepted only if it passes reliability tests and if there exists a valid action chain that reaches the goal using the available tools and prerequisites.
symbols: all procedural tests on the environment succeed
a valid sequence of tool actions reaches the task goal
whether the synthesized task is added to the training set

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Task goal: 'email the completed budget file'.
First draft world has an editor and an email tool, but no login action for the email account.
Procedural tests pass for editing, but executable path check fails for sending.
Dependency expansion adds account setup and login tools.
Now the full action chain exists, so the task is kept.

math.note: The second condition is essential because a task description is not enough; the system keeps it only when the action sequence really exists.

bars.h2: What changes when environment diversity scales

charts.title: Limited environment generation
charts.note: Small curated sets stay reliable, but they do not expose the agent to enough variation to generalize well.

charts.title: ScaleEnv
charts.note: ScaleEnv preserves task validity while broadening practice, so the agent improves on unseen multi-turn tool-use benchmarks because it trains on more verified action patterns.

items.html: A world can pass short checks and still fail after many actions if a later state update is wrong.
If each tool introduces several new prerequisites, the generator may create very deep chains that are hard to finish within a practical episode budget.
Large scale alone does not guarantee useful variety; if many domains share the same action pattern, the agent may still overfit.
The approach works when verification stays strict and domain templates stay varied, because then each accepted task is both solvable and genuinely different from the others.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny environment generator for office-style tool use. Let it create tasks such as editing a file, searching records, sending a message, or updating a calendar. Add a procedural tester that checks each tool's state change, and add a dependency expander that inserts prerequisites such as login or file creation when they are missing. Show that the final accepted tasks solve reliably under scripted rollouts and that an agent trained on more diverse verified worlds handles held-out domains better because it has practiced more kinds of action chains.
demo.closing: The demo should make clear that larger training sets help only when the worlds are verified, because broken environments teach the wrong lesson while diverse working environments let the agent practice reusable planning behavior.
